title: 03 · Test
section: “Will we really use 78% of System C’s output?”
text:
“Will we really use 78% of System C’s output?”
Simple payback favours System A at about 2.92 years. A 20-year discounted cash-flow view tells a different story: under the base assumptions, System C has the highest NPV at about R2.871 million.
Why? Payback focuses on recovery speed. NPV considers the value today of future net savings over the full analysis period.
The Production Manager now questions System C’s 78% self-consumption. Your task is to stress-test that assumption.

title: Should We Invest in Solar?
text:
What is this activity about?
This micro-learning activity develops your ability to use spreadsheet technology to support a commercial capital-investment decision in a South African business context. You will work with financial and operational information, build and interrogate a spreadsheet model, compare alternatives and communicate a reasoned recommendation.
The purpose is not simply to learn spreadsheet formulas. The purpose is to develop applied digital, analytical and decision-making competence: using a digital tool appropriately, understanding the assumptions behind the output, and exercising judgement when the evidence is incomplete.

title: Should We Invest in Solar?
text:
Learning outcomes
On successful completion of this activity, you should be able to:

Interpret financial and operational information relevant to a capital-investment decision.
Construct a structured spreadsheet model using appropriate formulas, cell references and number formats.
Calculate and compare useful generation, annual savings and simple payback across alternative proposals.
Use and interpret discounted cash-flow information and sensitivity analysis to evaluate the effect of changing a material assumption.
Create an appropriate visualisation that communicates decision-relevant information clearly.
Evaluate assumptions and supplier claims using professional scepticism and identify additional evidence required.
Formulate and communicate a concise, evidence-based recommendation that recognises commercial trade-offs and uncertainty.
Reflect on the strengths and limitations of the model and transfer the modelling approach to another business decision.

The activity follows one unfolding management problem through five stages: Understand → Build → Test → Decide → Reflect. A short Spreadsheet Essentials bridge supports learners who are new to Excel or Google Sheets.

title: Should We Invest in Solar?
section: Cape Manufacturing has a capital-allocation decision to make
text:
Cape Manufacturing has a capital-allocation decision to make
Cape Manufacturing is a Western Cape industrial producer. Electricity is a material operating cost, tariffs are expected to rise, and management is considering rooftop solar PV as a way to reduce grid purchases and improve energy resilience.
Three suppliers have submitted proposals. Each looks attractive for a different reason. The Financial Director does not want a sales comparison; she wants a transparent commercial analysis that can be challenged before capital is committed.
You are the Junior Commercial Analyst / Trainee Accountant. You have been asked to turn the proposals into an Excel model, test a key assumption and prepare a concise recommendation.

title: 01 · Understand
text: Open course in new window ↗

title: 01 · Understand
text:
Before you open the spreadsheet …
Which measure would you inspect first if you had to advise the Financial Director?
 Installed cost  System size  Gross generation  Annual saving  Payback

Your choice is saved automatically on this device. You will revisit it on Reflect.

title: 01 · Understand
section: Price is only one part of the decision
text:
Price is only one part of the decision
A larger PV system can generate more electricity, but Cape Manufacturing only saves money on solar electricity it can use when it is produced. This makes self-consumption the bridge between technical output and economic value.
If a system generates 100 kWh while the factory can use only 80 kWh, its self-consumption is 80%. In this simplified case, unused generation has no economic value.

title: 04 · Decide
text:
Open course in new window ↗
There is no single acceptable recommendation if the reasoning is coherent, quantified and appropriately qualified.

title: 04 · Decide
section: The spreadsheet gives evidence. It does not choose the decision rule.
text:
The spreadsheet gives evidence. It does not choose the decision rule.
You now have a genuine commercial trade-off. Management needs a recommendation that distinguishes measured results from assumptions still requiring verification.

title: Reviewer Rationale
text:
Constructive alignment is made visible
The activity is organised around explicit intended learning outcomes, authentic learning activities, formative checkpoints, associated assessment criteria and observable evidence of achievement. The narrative is the professional context through which the outcomes are developed; it does not replace the curriculum structure.
The design deliberately integrates foundational competence (understanding concepts and assumptions), practical competence (performing spreadsheet and analytical tasks) and reflexive competence (adapting reasoning, evaluating uncertainty and transferring learning).
The activity is best described as designed in accordance with South African outcomes-based and constructive-alignment principles. It should not be represented as independently “CHE accredited” or as an NQF-registered qualification. Exact formal module-level alignment would require the approved Stellenbosch module outcomes, assessment plan and institutional curriculum documentation.

title: Reviewer Rationale
section: One case, one evolving model, one professional decision
text:
One case, one evolving model, one professional decision
The activity is structured as a continuous workplace narrative. The learner receives imperfect supplier information, constructs a transparent spreadsheet model, encounters a challenge to an assumption, stress-tests the model, communicates a recommendation and reflects on transfer.
The five-step arc is Understand → Build → Test → Decide → Reflect. The separate Spreadsheet Essentials bridge supports true beginners in either Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets without turning the activity into a generic software tutorial.

title: Reviewer Rationale
text:
SAICA competency alignment
This activity is designed to evidence publicly documented SAICA competencies associated with the former CA2025 framework, now described by SAICA as the CA of the Future Competency Framework. It particularly integrates:


Digital acumen
Digital user skills: using technology as an enabler of decision-making; data analysis and spreadsheet modelling; deliberate use of formulas, references and visual communication.


Decision-making acumen
Analytical and critical thinking, weighing alternatives, integrated thinking, numerical reasoning and judgement.


Professional scepticism
Questioning supplier assumptions and unsupported claims, identifying evidence gaps and withholding reliance until appropriate evidence is obtained.



Why this is Digital- and Leadership Acumen
Digital acumen is treated as more than software proficiency. The learner uses a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets) to structure information, make logic auditable, interrogate uncertainty and communicate evidence. Leadership/professional acumen enters when the learner must make a qualified recommendation despite competing criteria and incomplete evidence.

Alignment note: this is a non-credit application demonstration. The public sources support alignment with Stellenbosch’s Digital- and Leadership Acumen context and SAICA’s competency language, but exact module-level constructive alignment would require the formally approved module outcomes and assessment plan.

title: Reviewer Rationale
text:
Publicly documented curriculum context

Stellenbosch School of Accountancy includes Digital- and Leadership Acumen modules in its accountancy programmes, including modules focused on data analytics for accountants.
SAICA defines digital user skills as using technology ethically to optimise decision-making and business efficiencies, and defines decision-making competencies including analytical thinking, critical thinking, integrated thinking and judgement.
SAICA describes professional scepticism as questioning information, remaining alert to possible error or fraud, and critically evaluating evidence.

Sources for reviewer verification: SAICA CA of the Future / Competencies Defined; SAICA IAC competency framework; Stellenbosch School of Accountancy programme information.


Platform design rationale


Spreadsheet reasoning is the competence; software menus are scaffolding
The activity deliberately preserves identical formulas, sheet names and cell addresses across Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Platform-specific guidance is limited to interface operations such as opening/saving, number formatting, filling formulas and chart creation.
This allows the learner to demonstrate transferable digital acumen rather than success being contingent on prior familiarity with one vendor interface.




V7 interaction design


Interactivity is tied to evidence of learning
The interactive elements are deliberately sparse and purposeful: a pre-model prediction activates prior conceptions; formula reveals support guided practice; management messages maintain authentic workplace narrative; sensitivity interpretation requires judgement rather than calculation alone; the pre-submission checklist makes assessment criteria visible; and the final reflection closes the prediction-feedback-transfer loop.
Decorative interaction has been avoided. Each interaction either elicits evidence, provides formative feedback, scaffolds performance or strengthens transfer.



Design principle: technical spreadsheet skills are introduced at the point where the case creates a reason to use them.
